# C. elegans transgenerational avoidance of P. fluorescens is mediated by the Pfs1 sRNA and vab-1

**Authors:** Renee J Seto; Rachel Brown; Rachel Kaletsky; Lance R Parsons; Rebecca S Moore; Julia M Balch; Zemer Gitai; Coleen T Murphy

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA. | 2LSI Genomics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA.

## Abstract

In its natural habitat, Caenorhabditis elegans must distinguish friend from foe. Pseudomonas are abundant in the worm’s environment and can be nutritious or pathogenic. Previously, we found that worms learn to avoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Pseudomonas vranovensis through a small RNA (sRNA)–mediated pathway targeting the C. elegans gene maco-1, and this behavior is inherited for four generations. Here, we show that C. elegans learns to transgenerationally avoid another pathogenic bacteria Pseudomonas fluorescens 15 (PF15). The PF15 sRNA, Pfs1, targets the VAB-1 ephrin receptor through 16 nt of perfect match, suggesting the evolution of a distinct bacterial sRNA/C. elegans gene target pair. Knockdown of both maco-1 and vab-1 induce PF15 avoidance, and vab-1 loss reduces maco-1 expression, placing both genes in the sRNA-targeted pathogenic avoidance pathway. Thus, multiple genes in this avoidance pathway can act as targets for bacterial sRNAs, expanding the possibilities for evolution of trans-kingdom regulation of C. elegans behavior.

## Abstract

C. elegans’ TEI of learned pathogen avoidance is induced by a third bacterial small RNA, Pfs1, from P. fluorescens 15.

## INTRODUCTION

In their natural environment, Caenorhabditis elegans are exposed to a variety of bacterial food sources, some of which are pathogens. This microbe-rich environment has shaped C. elegans evolution, and ingestion of both nutritious and pathogenic bacteria can induce long-lasting molecular and behavioral changes in the worm, including changes in the behavior of the treated animals (P0) or their immediate progeny (F1) in intergenerational effects (1–5). Our laboratory previously demonstrated that worms not only learn to avoid pathogenic PA14 but also pass on this learned avoidance behavior to their progeny for four generations (6). Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance (TEI) is a mechanism by which parental experiences are passed on to progeny, optimizing their behaviors for the environmental conditions experienced by their ancestors. Parental experiences and environmental factors lead to heritable changes in the gene expression and behavior of subsequent generations in a variety of organisms, including plants (7), worms (6, 8–10), flies (11), and mice (12, 13). In C. elegans, TEI plays a role in a variety of processes, including antiviral activity (14) and bacterial pathogen avoidance (6, 8–10).

Our laboratory previously found that C. elegans can pass on small RNA (sRNA)–mediated learned avoidance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA14) or Pseudomonas vranovensis (GRb0427) to four generations of progeny through a molecular mechanism that requires an intact germline and neuronal signaling (6, 8–10). This process is initiated by ingestion of specific bacterial sRNAs and requires components of the RNA inheritance pathway, including SID-2, DCR-1, SID-1, HRDE-1, NRDE-4 (6, 8, 10), RDE-1, RDE-2, RDE-4, and MUT-7 (6, 8); the RNA-dependent RNA polymerases RRF-1 and RRF-3 (6, 8); P-granule, piRNA regulators, and germline genes, including PRG-1 (6), and MEG-3;MEG-4 (6); and COMPASS (Complex Proteins Associated with Set1) complex and chromatin components, including SET-2, SET-25, SET-32, HPL-2, RBR-2, and WDR-5.1 (6). Cer1 retrotransposon-encoded virus-like particles are also required (9), likely for germ line to neuron signaling, culminating in maco-1 down-regulation and subsequent up-regulation of the transforming growth factor–β (TGF-β) ligand daf-7 in the ASI amphid sensory neurons (6, 8–10). Both P. aeruginosa P11 and P. vranovensis Pv1 sRNAs have perfect sequence matches to exons of the C. elegans gene maco-1. Upon training with PA14, P. vranovensis, P11, or Pv1, maco-1 transcripts are down-regulated, resulting in up-regulation of daf-7 expression and subsequent avoidance behavior (8, 10).

Here, we show that transgenerational avoidance behavior can also be induced by another pathogenic bacteria strain from the worm’s natural habitat, Pseudomonas fluorescens 15 (PF15). PF15 was originally isolated from the rhizosphere of rice fields but belongs to a group of common soil bacterium that have been identified in the C. elegans microbiome (15, 16). Here, we show that the transgenerational inheritance of PF15 avoidance lasts four generations after bacterial lawn training before preference returns to naïve levels. Uniquely, C. elegans’ avoidance of PF15 requires the bacterial sRNA Pfs1, which targets the C. elegans gene vab-1. PF15, PF15 sRNAs, and Pfs1 sRNA training all induce daf-7 expression in the ASI neuron pair, and the SID-1 double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) transporter and Cer1 virus-like particles are required for transgenerational learned avoidance, indicating that the previously-described molecular mechanisms of TEI are used by PF15 as well. Knockdown of vab-1 in adult C. elegans, like sRNA or Pfs1 treatment, induces avoidance of PF15; knockdown of maco-1 also induces PF15 avoidance; and PF15 training and Pfs1 treatment both reduce maco-1 expression. Together, these data point to the role of VAB-1 and MACO-1 function in a shared pathway regulating pathogen avoidance. Thus, C. elegans appears to have evolved the ability to avoid several different pathogenic Pseudomonas species transgenerationally and through a shared molecular pathway, but through independent examples of bacterial sRNA–C. elegans neuronal gene matches that begin to delineate a signaling pathway for sRNA-mediated transgenerational inheritance of learned pathogen avoidance.

## RESULTS

### PF15 is pathogenic to C. elegans and induces learned avoidance

P. fluorescens (PF15) is present in C. elegans’ natural habitat (15, 16). PF15 is notable for its fluorescence in UV light due to its production of pyoverdine, a fluorescent siderophore (Fig. 1A) (17). PF15 is pathogenic to C. elegans: upon exposure to PF15, the worms become ill, their bodies shrink (Fig. 1B), and their life span is dramatically reduced (Fig. 1C; median survival = 40 hours; P < 0.0001), while control (OP50)–raised worms will continue to live for an average of 2 to 3 weeks. The innate immunity gene irg-1 is strongly induced upon exposure to PF15 (Fig. 1, D and E), as is also observed upon exposure to P. aeruginosa PA14 (6). By contrast, another natural pathogen, P. vranovensis, does not induce a strong innate immune response (10), suggesting that C. elegans can have different immune responses to different Pseudomonas pathogens.

Despite its pathogenicity, naive C. elegans show a slight naïve preference to PF15 over the laboratory strain of nonpathogenic Escherichia coli (OP50) (Fig. 1F, gray bar). This naïve attraction is similar to that observed previously for other natural bacterial strains (6, 10). However, after 24 hours of exposure to a PF15 lawn (“training”; fig. S1), when worms are presented again with PF15, now C. elegans robustly avoid PF15 (Fig. 1F, green bar), similar to learned avoidance after treatment with either PA14 (6) or P. vranovensis (10). The innate immunity regulator pmk-1 is not required for this learned avoidance after training on PF15 bacterial plates (Fig. 1G), suggesting that other pathway(s) may be functional in P0 avoidance besides innate immunity–induced avoidance; previously, we showed that innate immune avoidance and sRNA-mediated learned avoidance of PA14 are independent and additive for avoidance behavior in the P0 generation (8). Together, these data show that C. elegans uses both innate immune and noninnate immune pathways to respond to the pathogen PF15 in the P0 generation.

### PF15 induces transgenerational epigenetic inheritance of avoidance

Similar to P. aeruginosa (PA14)– and P. vranovensis (GRb0427)–induced transgenerational epigenetic inheritance (TEI) of avoidance behavior (6, 10), 24 hours of exposure to PF15 also induces C. elegans’ TEI of pathogen avoidance behavior (Figs. 1F and 2, A and B). This learned avoidance behavior in P0 mothers is passed on to progeny for four generations without any additional training (Fig. 2, A and B, and fig. S1), while fifth generation (F5) descendants resume naïve behavior, no longer avoiding PF15 (Fig. 2, A and B). As we previously observed with PA14 training, the magnitude of P0 avoidance is greater than the avoidance in subsequent generations (Fig. 2B), suggesting an additive avoidance response in the P0, but F1 to F4 responses are consistent before dropping in the F5 generation back to the naïve attraction shown by untrained animals.

### PF15 training induces DAF-7/TGF-β expression in mothers and progeny

Neuronal function is required for the sensing and subsequent avoidance of pathogenic bacteria strains (1, 2, 6, 8, 18). Neuronal expression of the TGF-β ligand daf-7 is dramatically induced upon PA14 or P. vranovensis exposure: In mothers (P0) exposed to PA14, daf-7 expression is induced in both the ASI and ASJ neurons (1), and their progeny (F1) exhibit increased daf-7 expression specifically in the ASI neurons (6). PA14 sRNAs, P11 sRNA (6, 8), P. vranovensis sRNAs, or Pv1 sRNA (10) exposure also induce daf-7p::GFP fluorescence in the ASI in P0 through F4 generations, indicating that the ASI expression of daf-7 is indicative of sRNA-mediated avoidance, while ASJ expression of daf-7 is a response to bacterial metabolites (1, 6) . Therefore, we were curious whether daf-7 expression also correlates with inheritance of PF15 avoidance. Worms exposed to a lawn of PF15 increase expression of daf-7p::GFP in the both the ASI and the ASJ neurons in the P0 generation (Fig. 2C), as we previously found for PA14 (6). Furthermore, expression of daf-7p::GFP in the ASI remains elevated in the F1 generation (Fig. 2C), which correlates with their F1 avoidance behavior (Fig. 2A) (6, 8, 10). The expression of daf-7 in the ASJ is notably absent in the F1 generation, as we observed for PA14, perhaps indicating a P0-only ASJ daf-7 expression response to PF15’s pyoverdine metabolite. These results are consistent with our previous findings that elevated daf-7 levels specifically in the ASI correlate with TEI of learned avoidance of PA14 and P. vranovensis (6, 10).

Because ASI function has been implicated in transgenerational inheritance of learned pathogen avoidance both in previous work and by our daf-7p::gfp results, we tested an ASI caspase (genetic ablation) strain for its naïve preference for PF15 versus OP50 and found that loss of the ASI greatly increases avoidance of PF15 (Fig. 2D). Therefore, our results suggest that ASI function is key for normal preference for PF15.

### PF15 avoidance can be transmitted horizontally

We previously discovered that media conditioned by grandprogeny (F2) of trained worms is sufficient to confer avoidance of PA14 or P. vranovensis to naïve worms through secretion and uptake of Cer1 virus-like particles (9, 10). To test whether PF15 avoidance could also be transferred horizontally, we obtained media conditioned by day 1 F2 grandprogeny of OP50- or PF15-trained mothers and used it to train naïve animals (Fig. 2D). Naïve worms exposed to conditioned media from the PF15-trained F2s avoided PF15, while worms exposed to conditioned media from their OP50-trained counterparts did not (Fig. 2D). Thus, as with PA14 and P. vranovensis, PF15 learned avoidance can horizontally spread through a population of worms.

### PF15-derived sRNAs induce learned pathogen avoidance and TEI behavior without illness

Because purified sRNAs isolated from PA14 and P. vranovensis are both sufficient and necessary to induce transgenerational avoidance of PA14 and P. vranovensis, and we observe similar mechanisms and F1-F4 TEI of learned PF15 avoidance, we were curious whether sRNAs from PF15 also regulate the transgenerational avoidance of PF15. To test this hypothesis, we first isolated sRNAs (<200 nt) from PF15 or OP50 (control) lawns (see Materials and Methods). We then trained worms by adding these purified sRNAs to an OP50 E. coli lawn for 24 hours. Worms trained on sRNAs from either OP50 or PF15 for 24 hours are healthy (Fig. 3A), yet PF15-derived sRNA training was sufficient to induce learned avoidance behavior in the trained worms (Fig. 3B). The magnitude of the sRNA-dependent response in P0 animals is smaller than the lawn training P0 response (Figs. 1F and 3B), consistent with an additive effect of innate immune response and sRNA response in the P0 generation (Fig. 3C) that we similarly observed with PA14 (8). PA14 and P. vranovensis sRNA-mediated avoidance both require Cer1 retrotransposon-encoded virus-like particles. Cer1 acts at the step of information transfer from the germ line to neurons, upstream of daf-7 regulation (9). We were curious whether PF15 sRNA-mediated avoidance also requires Cer1. We found that Cer1(gk870313) mutants trained on PF15 sRNA are unable to learn to avoid PF15 (Fig. 3D), suggesting that Cer1 is required for transmission of sRNA-based information from the germ line to neurons, as it is for PA14- and P. vranovensis–induced avoidance (9, 10).

We then tested the progeny of OP50 or PF15 sRNA-trained worms and found that PF15 avoidance lasts for four additional generations (F1 to F4; Fig. 3, E and F), mimicking the effect we observed on PF15 lawn training (Fig. 2, A and B).

Together, these results suggest that the mechanism for PF15 sRNA-mediated avoidance in mothers and their progeny is similar to that observed for PA14-induced avoidance (6, 8, 9). The fact that purified sRNAs are sufficient to induce avoidance of PF15 in the absence of intact pathogen suggests that PF15 sRNA-induced avoidance does not require virulence. Thus, sRNA-mediated learned avoidance functions independently of and additively with the innate immune response in the mother generation, and sRNA-mediated learned avoidance alone is transgenerationally inherited.

### Identification of PF15 sRNAs required for PF15 avoidance

Our results suggested that PF15-induced TEI of avoidance is mediated by sRNAs, but the specific sRNA required for this avoidance was unknown. Because there was no publicly available PF15 genome sequence that we could mine for information, we first purified, sequenced, and annotated the PF15 genome (Fig. 4A; BioProject PRJNA1114673; see Materials and Methods). Because the simplest model is that PF15 may contain one of the same sRNAs we previously identified in other Pseudomonas strains, we BLASTed the sequences of P11 and Pv1 against the PF15 genome, but we found no significant sequence similarity to either. Next, because P11 and Pv1 both target the C. elegans maco-1 gene with a 17- and 16-nt stretches of perfect match to maco-1 (8, 10), respectively, we also BLASTed the sequence of maco-1 against the PF15 genome but found no hits within intergenic regions, where sRNAs are usually found (19, 20). This was in contrast to P. vranovensis, which like P11, encodes a sRNA, Pv1, in an intergenic region; Pv1 also has no similarity to P11 but does have a 16-nt match to exon 1 of maco-1 (10), while P11 has a 17-nt perfect match to exon 8 of maco-1 (8, 10). Together, these results suggested that neither P11 nor Pv1 is the sRNA responsible for inducing TEI of PF15 avoidance and that the relevant PF15 sRNA targets a C. elegans gene other than maco-1.

To narrow our search for sRNAs that might target C. elegans genes, we then predicted gene locations and identified the intergenic regions in PF15, indicating possible locations of sRNAs, as we had found for Pv1 in the P. vranovensis genome (19, 20). Of these intergenic regions, we then determined which had ≥16 nt of perfect sequence match to C. elegans genes, resulting in a list of 11,423 intergenic regions and their corresponding C. elegans genes.

To identify candidate sRNAs that might be responsible for PF15’s induction of transgenerational avoidance, we tested PF15 grown under three different conditions. We found that sRNAs isolated from 25°C plate (our usual growth condition), 37°C plate, and 37°C liquid growth conditions all induced avoidance (Fig. 4B). These results contrast with PA14, which only induces avoidance when bacteria are grown on plates at 25°C, allowing differential expression analysis to narrow down the set of possible candidates to only six sRNAs (8). Because all three conditions induced avoidance, we sequenced sRNAs from each sample (BioProject PRJNA1114673; see Materials and Methods) and then examined expressed sRNAs in the intersection between the three conditions, narrowing the list to 646 candidate sRNAs.

To identify C. elegans genes that might be a target for the PF15 sRNA, we isolated and compared mRNA from worms that had been trained on PF15 or OP50 control bacteria (Fig. 4C, BioProject PRJNA1114673; see Materials and Methods). Because previous target C. elegans gene maco-1 transcripts are down-regulated in worms treated with PA14 or P. vranovensis (10), we examined the list of genes that were down-regulated upon PF15 treatment, resulting in a list of 174 candidates. We also noted which of these candidates were also down-regulated in PA14-treated worms and those that overlap. These filtering steps resulted in a candidate list of 26 candidate intergenic regions that correspond to C. elegans genes (table S2).

Previously, we found that mutants or RNA interference (RNAi) knockdown of maco-1 increased naïve avoidance of PA14 (8). Therefore, to test whether any of these genes might be targets of PF15 sRNAs, we carried out a rapid candidate screen by measuring the naive avoidance of PF15 after candidate gene knockdown in adulthood (fig. S2A); only reduction of vab-1, which has a 16-nt match with an intergenic region of the PF15 genome (Fig. 4D), significantly affected naïve attraction to PF15. We found that reduction of vab-1 by adult-only RNAi knockdown does indeed increase naïve avoidance of PF15 (Fig. 4E). We also confirmed that vab-1 gene expression is significantly decreased (Log2FC = −0.4363014, adjusted P value = 0.0189176) in worms treated with PF15 in our RNA sequencing data (Fig. 4F, BioProject PRJNA1114673).

vab-1 encodes the only known ephrin receptor in C. elegans. vab-1 is expressed in many tissues of the developing larva (hypodermal cells, neuroblasts, neurons, and oocytes) and is required in development for coordinated cell movements and epidermal morphogenesis (21–24). vab-1 is expressed in adult neurons (25) as well as other tissues, but has no previously-reported functions in adults. To further test the possible role of vab-1 in PF15 avoidance, we obtained genetic loss-of-function mutants of vab-1 [vab-1(e2)]. As shown in Fig. 4G, vab-1 mutants can have severe morphological defects; by contrast, adult-only vab-1 RNAi treatment has no effects on morphology (Fig. 4H). Although vab-1(e2) mutants and worms treated with vab-1 RNAi show normal chemotaxis to the strong odorant benzaldehyde (fig. S3, A and B), indicating that their general chemosensory and mobility abilities are intact, upon testing these mutants in a choice assay between OP50 and PF15, we found that vab-1 mutants had a high naïve avoidance of PF15 compared to N2 (Fig. 4I). In addition, we found that exposure to PF15 did not further increase avoidance in these mutants (Fig. 4J), supporting our hypothesis that decreased levels of vab-1 lead to PF15 avoidance. Thus, similar to the high naïve avoidance of PA14 by maco-1 mutants and maco-1 RNAi-treated animals (8), vab-1 RNAi and vab-1 mutants show high naïve avoidance of PF15 and an inability to learn further avoidance upon treatment with PF15.

### Pfs1 sRNA causes transgenerational PF15 avoidance and contains a match to C. elegans gene vab-1

To test if the PF15 intergenic region we identified as having a match with the C. elegans vab-1 gene caused avoidance, we cloned the 600–base pair (bp) intergenic fragment of the PF15 genome containing the vab-1 match region into E. coli and used this bacterial strain to train worms, as previously described (8, 10). We found that worms trained on E. coli expressing the intergenic region learned to avoid PF15 from P0 to F4 (Fig. 5A and fig. S3F).

To identify the sRNA with vab-1 homology expressed within the intergenic region, we examined our sRNA sequencing data (Fig. 4B) and observed that there are reads covering the region between a sulfate permease (SuIP) family inorganic anion transporter and a type VI secretion system tip protein, with an sRNA of ~200 nt that includes the 16 nt of sense vab-1 homology; we named this sRNA Pfs1 (Fig. 5B). To precisely define the ends of the Pfs1, we used rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) to sequence the 5′ and 3′ ends of this sRNA; RACE results determined that Pfs1 is 207-nt long (Fig. 5B). Once the precise ends of the sRNA had been defined, we generated predicted secondary structures for the Pfs1 sRNA (Fig. 5C); models with the lowest free energy (ΔG = −52.31) predicted that the 16-nt match (green region) lies in a stem loop, as was previously predicted for the match regions of the P11 and Pv1 sRNA structures (8, 10).

To test Pfs1 directly for its effects on C. elegans, we cloned the Pfs1 sRNA into E. coli and then trained worms on this E. coli–expressing Pfs1. We found that Pfs1 induced avoidance of PF15 in P0 (Fig. 5D), confirming that it is the sRNA responsible for inducing avoidance and does so from the P0 to F4 generations before returning to naïve preference in F5 (Fig. 5E), as we had seen with our lawn and total sRNA training (Figs. 1F; 2, A and B; and 3, D and E). Once again, we note that training on the sRNA alone (Pfs1) induces the same level of avoidance in P0 as in F1 to F4 (Fig. 5E), suggesting that there is no additional innate immunity–mediated avoidance in the P0 in response to Pfs1 sRNA. Pfs1-trained animals (fig. S3C) do not exhibit the morphological defects of the vab-1 mutants (Fig. 4G), consistent with our adult-only vab-1 RNAi observations (Fig. 4H).

We previously found that sid-1 mutants, which are defective in systemic RNAi, are unable to learn sRNA-mediated PA14 and P. vranovensis avoidance (8, 10). Similarly, sid-1(qt9) mutants are unable to learn PF15 avoidance from Pfs1 training (Fig. 5F), suggesting that Pfs1 sRNA also requires systemic RNAi for its effects. Thus, the Pfs1 sRNA appears to induce PF15 avoidance through a similar mechanism of dsRNA processing (26, 27), as previously shown for PA14 and P. vranovensis (8–10).

We next wondered if Pfs1 training was responsible for the increase in ASI daf-7p::gfp levels we had observed in PF15 lawn and total sRNA training. Indeed, we found that training worms on Pfs1-expressing bacteria for 24 hours significantly increased ASI daf-7p::gfp levels compared to control-trained worms (Fig. 5G), and the grandprogeny (F2) of trained P0 mothers retained this increased ASI daf-7p::gfp expression (Fig. 5H). The daf-7p::GFP expression that was induced in the ASJ by PF15 training (Fig. 2C) is not observed in Pfs1-trained animals, consistent with daf-7p::gfp being induced in the ASJ of P0s by PF15 metabolites rather than by sRNAs. Further, Pfs1 sRNA-induced daf-7 expression in the ASI of mothers (Fig. 5G) is transgenerationally inherited in the F2 grandprogeny (Fig. 5H). Thus, exposure to the sRNA Pfs1 is sufficient to induce both transgenerational avoidance of PF15 and transgenerational ASI daf-7p::gfp expression.

Some alleles of vab-1 display an abnormal lateral positioning of the ASI axon (28). We were curious if Pfs1 training altered localization of the ASI axon in addition to inducing daf-7 expression (i.e., whether the change in behavior is due to a change in axon morphology). We stained P0 and F1 control or Pfs1 sRNA-trained day 1 wild-type worms with DiI to label amphid neurons and saw no differences in axon localization (fig. S3D). Thus, the behavioral changes we observed do not require changes in axon positioning, which is consistent with the adult-induced dynamic changes in the ASI in response to PF15 or Pfs1 sRNA exposure, rather than developmental defects.

The ASI neuron is required for other behavioral phenotypes, including chemotaxis to lysine and plays a role in regulating dispersal behavior (29, 30). We tested ASI-ablated worms and found that, consistent with previously published results, these worms are defective in chemotaxis to lysine (fig. S3E); similarly, Pfs1-trained animals show a reduction in lysine chemotaxis (fig. S3E). ASI-ablated animals also show a significant increase in short reversals (Fig. 5I), as previously shown in studies of dispersal behavior (29); this behavior is also demonstrated by vab-1 RNAi-treated animals (Fig. 5J) and Pfs1-trained animals (Fig. 5K). Moreover, this behavior is inherited in the F1 progeny (Fig. 5L) and F2 grandprogeny (Fig. 5M) of Pfs1-trained P0 animals. These data are consistent with changes in ASI function being the basis of the Pfs1-mediated switch from attraction to avoidance of PF15.

### The 16 nucleotides of perfect vab-1 match in Pfs1 are necessary and sufficient for transgenerational PF15 avoidance

We hypothesize that Pfs1-mediated avoidance requires targeting and knockdown of vab-1 through the 16-nt perfect match in the Pfs1 stem loop. Therefore, we wanted to test if vab-1 is required for learned avoidance that is mediated by Pfs1 training. We found that vab-1(e2) mutants trained on control bacteria (naïve) already avoided PF15 to a level equivalent to Pfs1-trained N2 (Fig. 6A), as we previously observed in OP50-trained vab-1 mutants (Fig. 4I). Pfs1 training did not further increase avoidance (Fig. 6A); thus, vab-1 is required for Pfs1-mediated avoidance of PF15.

These data indicate that we have identified the specific sRNA sufficient for transgenerational PF15 avoidance and, more precisely, that the 16 nucleotides of perfect vab-1 match dictate this inherited behavioral change.

We showed that Cer1(gk870313) mutants are unable to further learn avoidance after PF15 sRNA training (Fig. 3D); similarly, Cer1(gk870313) mutants were also unable to learn from Pfs1 training (Fig. 6F). Thus, the Pfs1 sRNA appears to induce PF15 avoidance through a similar mechanism of Cer1 germline-to-neuron signaling as PA14 and P. vranovensis (8–10).

We were curious if the 16 nucleotides of perfect sequence match between Pfs1 and C. elegans vab-1 are conserved in other C. elegans strains. We previously tested several wild isolates of C. elegans for their ability to carry out transgenerational avoidance of PA14, and we identified those producing Cer1 protein products that were capable of pathogen avoidance in the context of sRNA P11 training. Analysis of the vab-1 sequence showed that this 16-nt region is perfectly conserved across the wild isolate genomes (Fig. 6G). Moreover, the 17-nt region of P11 in P. aeruginosa PA14 (fig. ### vab-1 acts upstream of maco-1

Although both maco-1 and vab-1 are expressed in neurons, as far as we know, they have not been reported to interact with one another or share any phenotypes and therefore might act in separate, parallel pathways. In particular, vab-1 has been primarily associated with developmental phenotypes (21–24), while loss of maco-1 affects dauer formation, a developmental decision, as well as synaptic function and chemotaxis and thermotaxis behaviors in adults (31, 32). However, since the PF15 and Pfs1 learned avoidance and daf-7p::gfp phenotypes resemble those we observed with PA14, P. vranovensis, P11, and Pv1 treatments, we wondered whether vab-1 acts in the same pathway as maco-1, the gene targeted by both PA14’s P11 sRNA and P. vranovensis’ Pv1 sRNA.

First, we tested the naïve (untrained) avoidance of PF15, as we previously found that maco-1 mutants display a high naïve avoidance of PA14 (8). maco-1(ok3165) mutants also display high naïve avoidance of PF15 (Fig. 7A) despite the fact that the target of PF15 sRNA is vab-1, not maco-1. Similarly, maco-1 RNAi treatment of C. elegans induces high naïve avoidance of PF15 (Fig. 7B). Together, these data suggest that maco-1 is involved in C. elegans’ avoidance of PF15.

We hypothesized that maco-1 reduction might affect vab-1 expression or function; unexpectedly, however, our transcriptional analyses show that maco-1 is in fact down-regulated in PF15-treated worms (Fig. 7D; log2FC = −0.647352, adjusted P value = 0.0001186023), placing maco-1 downstream of vab-1. Conversely, PA14 treatment does not cause down-regulation of vab-1 [vab-1 expression log2FC = −0.1044, adjusted P value = 0.3056; (6)], again suggesting that vab-1 must lie upstream rather than downstream of maco-1. Quantitative expression analysis [quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR)] of F2 (grandprogeny) of Pfs1-treated animals show that maco-1 transcripts are down-regulated transgenerationally as well (Fig. 7E). That is, despite neither PF15 nor Pfs1 having any match to maco-1 that might suggest an RNAi-like mechanism at work, maco-1 transcripts are decreased in worms subjected to PF15 or Pfs1 training. These data suggest that PF15 and Pfs1 treatment results in down-regulation of vab-1, which in turn causes the reduction of maco-1 (Fig. 7F), and this down-regulation is also maintained transgenerationally.

### PF15 Pfs1 sRNA training causes PA14, P. vranovensis, and Pseudomonas mendocina avoidance

Following our discovery that PF15 and Pfs1 training decrease maco-1 transcription, we then wondered if worms trained on Pfs1 would also avoid P. aeruginosa PA14 and P. vranovensis (GRb0427) because that avoidance is mediated through maco-1 reduction as well. We previously found that the PA14 sRNA P11 and the P. vranovensis sRNA Pv1 both induce avoidance of PA14 and P. vranovensis through maco-1 knockdown (8, 10) and that sRNAs from either PA14 or P. vranovensis each induce avoidance of the other Pseudomonas species (10). We found that training on Pfs1 sRNA-expressing bacteria indeed caused avoidance of both PA14 (Fig. 7G) and P. vranovensis (Fig. 7H). Thus, exposure to sRNAs from one pathogenic Pseudomonas, PF15, causes protective avoidance of other pathogens in the environment because they share the same mechanism of learned avoidance. However, this process is restricted to Pseudomonas species, as avoidance of Serratia marcescens is not induced by PF15 training in P0 or F1 (fig. S4A).

Induced avoidance can also be detrimental: We previously showed that learned avoidance of pathogens (P. vranovensis) can also induce avoidance of nonpathogenic bacteria, such as P. mendocina (10), a nonpathogenic, beneficial food source. Similarly, here, we found that Pfs1-trained animals also avoid P. mendocina (MSPm1) (Fig. 7I). Therefore, “forgetting” this avoidance after a few generations would help the animals to resume foraging on beneficial Pseudomonas that serve as good sources of nutrition, underscoring the importance of using a reversible mechanism to avoid pathogenic bacteria.

### Reduction of Ephrin pathway components mimics vab-1 effects on PF15 avoidance

Because we identified a new phenotype of vab-1 down-regulation, we wondered if other genes that act in the ephrin signaling pathway are involved in PF15 avoidance. To test this, we treated adult N2 worms with RNAi against genes in the VAB-1 pathway. RNAi knockdown of the worm ephrin ligand vab-2/efn-1 induced avoidance of PF15 (Fig. 8A), mimicking the effect we observed with vab-1 reduction. We then explored the roles of more components of the Ephrin pathway, including other predicted ephrin ligands (EFN-2, EFN-3, and EFN-4), the SH2 and SH3 domain-containing adaptor protein regulator of the actin cytoskeleton NCK-1/SID-4, and the cytoskeletal effector WASP/WSP-1. Mutants of nck-1 and wsp-1, like vab-1 and vab-2, have axon guidance and developmental defects (21, 22, 33, 34), but these phenotypes are not induced upon post-developmental knockdown by RNAi, as we do here. We found that the reduction of efn-3, efn-4, nck-1, and wsp-1 all increased the naïve avoidance of PF15 (Fig. 8B), suggesting that these genes that act downstream of vab-1 may also play a role in the adult regulation of pathogen avoidance.

## DISCUSSION

Previously, we found that both P. aeruginosa (PA14) and P. vranovensis (GRb0427) encode sRNAs (P11 and Pv1, respectively) with short perfect matches to the C. elegans gene maco-1 that induce avoidance of those pathogens in the mother and four additional generations (6, 8–10). Here, we have found that a third Pseudomonas species from the worm’s habitat, P. fluorescens PF15, encodes yet a third sRNA (Pfs1) that targets a different C. elegans gene, vab-1, to induce avoidance and its transgenerational inheritance. While Pfs1 does not target maco-1 itself, treatment of C. elegans with PF15 or reduction of vab-1 through Pfs1 targeting results in the down-regulation maco-1, placing both genes in the same pathway to regulate transgenerational pathogen avoidance. These results suggest that C. elegans has evolved the ability to detect and use different sRNAs from multiple bacterial species through a shared sRNA processing mechanism. Similar to the PA14 and P. vranovensis transgenerational avoidance pathways, PF15 avoidance uses the SID-1 RNA transporter, Cer1 particles for germline-to-neuron signaling, and DAF-7 signaling in the ASI neurons, indicating that the molecular mechanisms for detection and processing of these three bacterial sRNAs are conserved. Here, we found that Pfs1 treatment caused an increase in ASI-mediated short reversals that is maintained transgenerationally; this increase in reversals provides a mechanistic understanding of how bacterial sRNA effects could cause the behavioral switch from attraction to avoidance. Pfs1 training causes PA14 and P. vranovensis avoidance, indicating that multiple C. elegans genes in this avoidance pathway can be targeted by bacterial sRNAs. The simultaneous induction of avoidance of nonpathogenic food source bacteria such as P. mendocina suggests that “forgetting” learned avoidance after F4 is likely to be a beneficial adaptation.

We have now identified three different sRNAs in three different Pseudomonas species that use three different short (16 to 17 nt) perfect match sequences to target three exons of two C. elegans genes that act in the same pathway (Fig. 8C). Our data further suggest that decreased VAB-1 function as a result of PF15 or Pfs1 treatment disrupts the transcription of the maco-1 gene, resulting in increased daf-7 expression and subsequent avoidance of PF15 (Fig. 8C). Therefore, we are now able to draw more conclusions about the origins, adaptive advantage, and scope of this trans-kingdom communication. C. elegans appears to have evolved a pathogen avoidance strategy that involves “reading” a Pseudomonas pathogen’s sRNAs as biomarkers of future illness by matching perfect sequences of genes involved in the pathogen avoidance behavior, including but perhaps not limited to vab-1 and maco-1. This may be beneficial in the wild, as exposure to one pathogenic Pseudomonas species may confer cross-species immunity through this sRNA-based mechanism. The resulting adaptive immune memory may provide a powerful survival advantage for subsequent progeny, allowing them to properly respond to a pathogenic threat without ever experiencing infection and illness, but still reduce this avoidance after four generations to prevent the accidental avoidance of beneficial food sources that “smell” similar to the pathogens (10).

Intriguingly, RNAi knockdown of vab-2, which encodes an Ephrin ligand, also results in PF15 avoidance. The fact that VAB-1 and VAB-2 are involved in this response suggests an adult role for the Ephrin axon guidance pathway in a secondary adult function, regulation of bacterial avoidance. While vab-1 mutants display defects in axon guidance and in development, maco-1 mutants are defective in a separate constellation of phenotypes, such as defects in isothermal tracking behavior and pheromone-induced dauer formation; sRNA-mediated bacterial avoidance switching in adulthood is a newly identified role for both these genes. In fact, WSP-1 has been shown to play a post-developmental role in synaptic function at the neuromuscular junction, suggesting that actin cytoskeleton dynamics may also be important for the processes we are studying (33). Furthermore, the RNAi defective mutant sid-4 was identified as nck-1 (35), suggesting that in addition to the components of the RNAi pathway that we had already implicated in learned pathogen avoidance (SID-1 and SID-2), Ephrin signaling components that have RNA interference phenotypes and regulate the actin cytoskeleton might be important for the process. We recently found that several axon guidance genes also play a role in the regulation of long-term memory both in worms and in mice, suggesting a previously unappreciated role for these pathways in adult behavioral functions (36). Thus, genes that are considered primarily “developmental” may in fact have secondary behavioral functions that only emerge in adulthood.

The discovery of a third bacterial sRNA-C. elegans gene match that acts in the same pathway but not through maco-1 suggests that the phenomenon is not only conserved, but also may be common among other bacterial species that C. elegans encounters in the wild—but that targets other than maco-1 may be involved. Thus, it is likely that other pathogenic Pseudomonas species in C. elegans’ environment also encode sRNAs that C. elegans interpret as biomarkers of future pathogenesis, perhaps targeting other genes in the vab-1/maco-1/daf-7 avoidance pathway. The consistency of C. elegans’ responses to sRNAs from Pseudomonas species found in the wild combined with the conservation of sites such as the 16-nt match with Pfs1 in vab-1 (as well as the perfect matches between P11 and Pv1 with maco-1) suggests that we have uncovered a robust and reproducible mechanism of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance that C. elegans has evolved to avoid pathogens without sacrificing nutritional resources.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Experimental model and subject details

#### Bacterial strains

PF15 was a gift from M. Donia’s laboratory. The GRb0427 strain was a generous gift from B. Samuel’s laboratory. E. coli OP50 was provided by the C. elegans Genetics Center (CGC). P. aeruginosa (PA14) was a gift from Z. Gitai’s laboratory. MSPm1 is part of the CeMbio collection and was obtained from the CGC (16). S. marcescens [American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) 274] was provided by the ATCC. Control (L44440), vab-1 maco-1, vab-2, efn-2, efn-3, efn-4, nck-1, wsp-1, and candidate screen (see table S2) RNAi were obtained from the Ahringer RNAi library, and sequences were verified.

E. coli expressing the 600-nt PF15 intergenic region containing the 16-nt match to vab-1 was constructed by Gibson assembly. The intergenic region was cloned out of PF15 and ligated into pZE27GFP using PCR to linearize the plasmid, DpnI digest, and a single fragment Gibson assembly to ligate. The plasmid was transformed into MG1655 E. coli using a standard transformation protocol: pZE27GFP (forward: GGTACCTTTGTCCTCTTTAATG); reverse: taagcttgatgggggatcc) and intergenic region (forward: GGGATCCCCCATCAAGCTTATAAGACTTTAACCGAAATTGTTAG; reverse: TTAAAGAGGACAAAGGTACCTCTTCGTTGCCTTCCATGC)].

E. coli expressing the Pfs1 sRNA was constructed in a similar method using primers specific to the Pfs1 region. Pfs1 was ligated into pZE27GFP using PCR to open the plasmid, DpnI digest, and a single fragment Gibson assembly to ligate. This plasmid was transformed into MG1655 E. coli using a standard transformation protocol: Pfs1 (forward: GGGATCCCCCATCAAGCTTATATTGCCATAA-ACGACTTCCTCTG; reverse: TTAAAGAGGACAAAGGTACCAATTGTTAGAGGTGATGCCCAAGT)].

Control bacteria for the intergenic region and Pfs1-expressing bacteria consisted of plasmid pZE27GFP transformed into MG1655 E. coli using a standard transformation protocol. The PF15 vab-1 mismatch was generated using an allelic exchange approach to create a strain with point mutations that disrupt homology to vab-1 by 5 bp but preserves predicted secondary structure of the sRNA. Generation of allelic exchange vectors was done by three-piece Gibson assembly (NEBuilder) using the pExG2 backbone (37) restriction digested with Hind III and Xba I (NEB) and inserts generated by PCR of PF15 genomic template followed by primer extension PCR to generate the desired mutant allele. The assembled vectors were transformed into the E. coli strain S17-1λpir (ATCC, #BAA-2428) for conjugation into PF15. Conjugation and subsequent selection for double crossover conjugants were done (38) with the following adaptations for use in PF15: The conjugation recipient culture of PF15 was grown at 37°C, and all subsequent growth steps were done at 30°C. Selective media following conjugation included carbenicillin (100 μg/ml) for donor counterselection as S17 is susceptible and PF15 is naturally resistant. Mutations were confirmed by colony PCR of the PF15 Pfs1 genomic region followed by Sanger sequencing: reverse primer to amplify upstream from mid pfs1 (CATCCACCACAGAGATGATC), forward primer to amplify downstream of mid pfs1 (CCCCTGACCCCGCGAG), reverse primer amplifying upstream of mid pfs1 adding point mutations homology arm (AAATGCTGTCCTAGCATCGGCGTACATCCACCACAGAGATG), forward primer amplifying downstream of mid pfs1 adding point mutations homology arm (GCCGATGCTAGGACAGCATTTCCCCTGACCCCGCGAG), and pfs1 sequencing primer (forward: GAGCATGGCGCAAGTAGC; reverse: GCTCCAGTTGCCAATCGTAG).

#### C. elegans strains

The following worm strains were provided by the CGC: N2 (wild type), AU133: agls17[Pmyo-2::mCherry + Pirg-1::GFP], KU25: pmk-1(km25), FK181: ksIs2 [Pdaf-7p::gfp + rol-6(su1006)], CQ759: maco-1(ok3165), HC196: sid-1(qt9), CB2: vab-1(e2), PY7505: oyIs84 [gpa-4p::TU#813 + gcy-27p::TU#814 + gcy-27p::GFP +unc-122p::DsRed], and CQ667: Cer1(gk870313) 6x outcrossed against N2 (9).

#### Cultivation of bacterial strains

E. coli OP50, P. fluorescens (PF15), P. aeruginosa (PA14), P. vranovensis, P. mendocina (MSPm1), and S. marcescens were cultured overnight (14 to16 hours) in LB [tryptone (10 g/liter), yeast extract (5 g/liter), and NaCl in distilled water (10 g/liter)] with shaking (250 rpm) at 37°C. E. coli expressing the intergenic region or Pfs1 sRNA and their respective control were cultured in LB supplemented with kanamycin (50 μg/ml) overnight (approximately 16 hours) with shaking (250 rpm) at 37°C. RNAi bacteria were grown in LB supplemented with carbenicillin (100 μg/ml) and tetracycline (12.5 μg/ml) overnight (approximately 16 hours) with shaking (250 rpm) at 37°C.

#### General maintenance of C. elegans strains

Worm strains were maintained at 20°C on high growth medium (HG) plates [NaCl (3 g/liter), Bacto Peptone (20 g/liter), and Bacto Agar in distilled water (30 g/liter), with cholesterol (4 ml/liter; 5 mg/ml in ethanol), 1 M CaCl2 (1 ml/liter), 1 M MgSO4 (1 ml/liter), and 1 M potassium phosphate buffer (25 ml/liter; pH 6.0) added to molten agar after autoclaving] on E. coli OP50 using standard methods.

#### Training plate preparation

Training plates were prepared by seeding 800 μl of bacteria onto NGM [NaCl (3 g/liter), Bacto Peptone (2.5 g/liter), and Bacto Agar in distilled water (17 g/liter), with cholesterol (1 ml/liter; 5 mg/ml in ethanol), 1 M CaCl2 (1 ml/liter), 1 M MgSO4 (1 mL/liter), and 1 M potassium phosphate buffer (25 ml/liter; pH 6.0) added to molten agar after autoclaving] or HG plates. PF15 and its control, E. coli OP50, were prepared on NGM plates to avoid pathogen overgrowth and grown at 25°C for 48 hours. sRNA producing MG1655 were prepared on HG plates [supplemented with kanamycin (50 μg/ml)] and grown at 25°C for 48 hours. For training with purified OP50 or PF15 sRNAs or horizontal transfer with conditioned media, 200 μl of OP50 was spotted in the center of a 6-cm NGM plate and incubated at room temperature for 48 hours. RNAi bacteria were prepared on HG plates [supplemented with 1 M isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG; 1 ml/liter) and carbenicillin (1 ml/liter; 100 mg/ml)] and kept at room temperature for 48 hours. All plates were left to cool on a benchtop for 1 hour to equilibrate to room temperature before the addition of worms.

#### Bacterial choice assay plate preparation

Overnight bacterial cultures of PF15 were diluted 1:2 in LB to an optical density (OD) at 600 = 1, and standard cultures of undiluted OP50 were used. PA14, GRb, S. marcescens, and MSPm1 were diluted 1:4 in LB. To prepare bacterial choice plates, 25 μl of each bacterial suspension was spotted onto opposite sides of a 6-cm NGM plate (see fig. S1). These plates were incubated for 2 days at 25°C and allowed to equilibrate to room temperature for 1 hour before performing the choice assay.

### Preparation of bacteria for RNA isolation

Bacterial lawns (plate) for RNA collection were cultured as previously described and grown for 2 days on plates at 25°C (or 37°C for sequencing). Liquid cultures (37°C liquid condition) for sequencing were pelleted for collection. Bacterial lawns were collected from the surface of NGM plates using a cell scraper. In brief, 1 ml of M9 buffer was applied to the surface of the bacterial lawn, and the bacterial suspension following scraping was transferred to a 15-ml conical tube. PF15 from 10 plates or OP50 from 15 plates was pooled in each tube and pelleted at 5000g for 10 min at 4°C. The supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was resuspended in 1 ml of TRIzol LS for every 100 μl of bacterial pellet recovered. The pellet was resuspended by vortexing and subsequently frozen at −80°C until RNA isolation.

### Bacterial sRNA isolation

To isolate RNA from bacterial pellets, TRIzol lysates were incubated at 65°C for 10 min with occasional vortexing. Debris was pelleted at 7000g for 5 min at 4°C. The supernatant was transferred to new tubes containing one-fifth the volume of chloroform. Samples were mixed thoroughly by inverting and centrifuged at 12,000g for 10 min at 4°C. The aqueous phase was used at input for RNA purification using the mirVana miRNA Isolation Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions for sRNA (<200 nt) isolation. Purified RNA was used immediately for sRNA training or frozen at −80°C until further use for sequencing.

### Worm preparation for training

Eggs from young adult hermaphrodite worms were obtained by bleaching and subsequently placed onto HG plates and incubated at 20°C for 2 days. Synchronized L4 worms (48–52 hours post-bleaching) were used in all training experiments.

For sRNA training, 100 μg of sRNA was added to the OP50 spot on the sRNA training plates. For RNAi, 200 μl of 0.1 M IPTG was spotted onto plates and left to dry at room temperature before adding worms. For horizontal training from conditioned media, 200 μl of conditioned media was added to an OP50 spot and allowed to dry completely.

Synchronized L4 worms were washed off plates using M9 and left to pellet on the bench top for 2 to 3 min. Then, 5 μl of worms were placed onto sRNA-spotted training plates, 10 or 40 μl of worms were plated onto OP50 or pathogen-seeded training plates, and 20 μl of worms were placed onto RNAi plates or MG1655 sRNA-expressing bacteria plates. Worms were incubated on training plates at 20°C in separate containers for 24 hours. After 24 hours, worms were washed off plates using M9 and washed an additional 2 to 3 times to remove excess bacteria. Worms were tested in the aversive learning assay or bleached to obtain the next generation of progeny (fig. S1).

### Aversive learning assay

On the day of the assay, choice assay plates were left at room temperature for 1 hour before use. To begin the assay, 1 μl of 1 M sodium azide was spotted onto each respective bacteria spot to be used as a paralyzing agent during choice assay and preserve first bacterial choice. Worms were washed off training plates in 2 ml of M9 into 1.5-ml tubes and allowed to pellet by gravity. Worms were washed two to three additional times in M9 until no bacteria visibly remained. Using a wide orifice pipet tip, 5 μl of worms (approximately 30 to 150 worms) were spotted at the bottom of the assay plate, midway between the bacterial lawns. Aversive learning assays were incubated at room temperature for 1 hour before manually counting the number of worms on each bacterial spot. Plating a large number of worms (>200) on choice assay plates was avoided because excess worms clump at bacterial spots, making it difficult to distinguish worms, and high densities of worms can alter behavior. Plates with fewer than 15 worms were censored. Worms paralyzed further than 0.5 cm from the bacterial spot were not counted: choice index = (# of worms on OP50 − # of worms on PF15)/(total # of worms) and learning index (calculated for each replicate) = (average choice index of PF15, PF15 sRNA, or intergenic region-trained worms) − (average choice index of control trained worms).

In experiments in which F1 and subsequent generations are used, day 1 worms from parental (P0) training (a separate cohort than those used for behavior) were bleached, and eggs were placed onto HG plates and left for 3 days at 20°C. After 3 days, the F1 worms (day 1 adults at 72 hours) were washed off HG plates with M9. Some of the pooled worms were subjected to an aversive learning assay, and the remaining worms were bleached to obtain eggs, which were then placed onto HG plates left at 20°C for 3 days and used to test the F2 generation. The same steps were followed for subsequent generations (fig. S1).

### Lysine chemotaxis assay

A solution of 2 M lysine (CAS 56-87-1) pH 6 was used for lysine chemotaxis assays. P0 worms were trained as described above, and all assays were performed on day 1 adults. One day before the assay, 15 μl of lysine solution or water (control) was added to two spots equidistant from an origin on 10-cm NGM plates. Three hours before the assay, an additional 15 μl of lysine solution or water was added to the same spots. This established a gradient such that N2 or control worms were able to sense the lysine spot. To start the assay, worms were washed off of plates (HG seeded with OP50 for N2 or ASI caspase or control or Pfs1-expressing bacteria for trained worms) with M9, allowed to settle, and washed an additional 1 to 2× until the M9 was free of bacteria. To begin the assay, 1 μl of 1 M sodium azide was added to the previously established lysine solution and water spots. Then, 5 μl of worms were added to the origin, equidistant from the established lysine and water spots. At 2 hours, worms within a 1 cm radius of each spot were counted as well as worms that had not reached either spot. A chemotaxis index was calculated for each plate (# worms at lysine − #worms at water control)/(#worms at lysine + #worms at water control + #worms elsewhere on plate).

### Dispersal (short reversal) assay

Worms were prepared as previously described by bleaching onto HG plates (Fig. 5I), adult-only RNAi treatment, or 24 hours adult training followed by bleaching for generations P0-F2. All assays were performed on day 1 adult worms. For each assay, a single worm was picked onto an unseeded 60-mm NGM plate equilibrated to room temperature. After 1 min of equilibration time, each worm was observed for the next 4 min (minutes 1 to 5 of the assay), and the number of short and long reversals were counted for each worm (short reversal < 3 head swings, long reversal ≥ 3 head swings), adapted from Gray et al. (29).

### Conditioned media preparation

F2 progeny of PF15 or OP50 grandmothers were obtained as described above. Day 1 adult F2 worms were washed off plates with M9, allowed to settle, and then washed an additional 1× in M9 before removing the supernatant. For every 50 μl of worm pellet, 300 μl of S-basal media was added. A 1.5 ml of the worm and S-Basal solution was transferred to each well of an untreated six-well plate and incubated for 24 hours at 20°C to produce conditioned media. After 24 hours, plates were inspected to ensure no worms had exploded, bagged, or died. Conditioned media was pooled into 15-ml conical tubes with wide-orifice pipette tips and cleared from bacteria by 6500g centrifugation for 10 min. The media was then passed through a 0.22-μm filter. Unconcentrated conditioned media (200 μl) was added to OP50 spots prepared as described above, allowed to dry, and used immediately to train 5 μl of naïve L4 worms. After 24 hours of training, these worms were tested in the choice assay as described above.

### Sequencing and annotating the PF15 genome

Genomic DNA was extracted from an overnight PF15 culture using the QIAGEN DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit for Gram-negative bacteria. Nanopore sequencing was performed by MIGS (now SeqCenter). Genome annotation was performed using Prodigal gene prediction software (39) and Standalone BLAST (BioProject PRJNA1114673).

### Bacterial sRNA sequencing

Each sample of PF15 sRNA was tested for C. elegans behavior before sequencing. The size distribution of sRNA samples was examined on a Bioanalyzer 2100 using RNA 6000 Pico chip (Agilent Technologies). The sRNA sequencing protocol was similar to the protocol previously used (10). Around 300 ng of sRNA from each sample was first treated with RNA 5′ pyrophosphohydrolase (New England Biolabs) at 37°C for 30 min and then converted to Illumina sequencing libraries using the PrepX RNA-seq library preparation protocol on the automated Apollo 324 NGS Library Prep System (Takara Bio). In brief, the treated RNA samples were ligated to two different adapters at each end and reverse-transcribed to cDNA and amplified by PCR using different barcoded primers. The libraries were examined on Bioanalyzer DNA High Sensitivity chips (Agilent) for size distribution, quantified by Qubit fluorometer (Invitrogen), and then pooled at equal molar amount and sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq 6000 S Prime flowcell as single-end 122-nt reads. The pass-filter reads were used for further analysis (BioProject PRJNA1114673).

### Bacterial sRNA sequencing data analysis

Two replicates of PF15 sRNA grown from 25°C plates were sequenced, five replicates of PF15 sRNA grown from 37°C plates were sequenced, and two replicates of PF15 sRNA grown from 37°C liquid were sequenced. Reads were mapped to the sequenced PF15 genome using RNA STAR (40). Default settings were used for the RNA STAR mapping. The resulting BAM files were then used to identify putative sRNAs.

### Whole worm mRNA isolation, sequencing, and analysis

Adult worms (P0) trained as described on E. coli OP50 or PF15 were collected in M9 and washed several times to remove excess bacteria. Worm pellets were crushed in liquid nitrogen and transferred to an appropriate volume of Trizol LS (100 μl of worm pellet in 900 μL of Trizol). Total RNA was extracted from Trizol using chloroform extraction, isopropanol and ethanol precipitation, and cleanup using the RNeasy mini kit. mRNA libraries for directional RNA sequencing were prepared using the SMARTer Apollo System and were sequenced (paired-end) on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform.

### RACE for Pfs1 sRNA identification

Three independent replicates of PF15 sRNA were isolated from PF15 grown on plates at 25°C as described above and purified using the mirVana miRNA Isolation Kit. Rapid Amplification of cDNA Ends (RACE) to determine bacterial sRNA 5′ and 3′ ends was performed as described (41). In brief, RNA was treated with DNase I, XRN-1 endoribonuclease, and RppH with phenol/chloroform extraction and ethanol precipitation between each enzymatic step. sRNAs were then ligated with T4 ligase, and cDNA was made using the SuperScript III First-Strand System with random hexamers. cDNA fragments were amplified with PCR primers specific to the internal region of Pfs1, gel purified, and cloned into the pCR4-TOPO vector before sequencing with M13F. Primers: Pfs1 RACE PCR (forward: CGCGAGACGGACGACTGACG; reverse: TCGCGGTACATCCACCACAGAG). ### Pfs1 structure prediction

A prediction of the secondary structure of the Pfs1 sRNA was made using the mFold tool on the UNAfold webserver (42).

### Imaging and image analysis

All images were taken on a Nikon Eclipse Ti microscope or Nikon A1 R confocal microscope. Day 1 worms were prepared and treated as described in “worm preparation for training.” Worms were mounted on 2% agar pads on glass slides and immobilized using 1 mM levamisole.

Differential inference contrast (DIC) images of whole worms following OP50 or PF15 lawn or sRNA training were imaged at 20× magnification following preparation and training as described in worm preparation for training. For green fluorescent protein (GFP)–transgenic worms, Z-stack multichannel (DIC and GFP) images were acquired at 20× magnification (irg-1p::gfp) or 60× magnification (dafp7p::gfp) magnification. For DiI staining, Z-stack multichannel (DIC and DiI) images were acquired at 60× magnification.

For DiI (1,1′-dioctadecyl-3,3,3′,3′-tetramethylindocarbocyanine perchlorate) staining and imaging, worms were prepared as previously described and transferred into a 1.5-ml Eppendorf tube with M9. Worms were allowed to settle, M9 was removed, and an additional 1 ml of M9 was added along with 5 μl of stock solution of DiI (2 mg/ml) in dimethyl formamide. Worms were incubated on a nutator with dye for 3 hours before being washed 2× in M9 to remove excess dye. For DiI representative images, maximum intensity projections were generated, and outlines were drawn on the basis of DIC images.

For irg-1p::gfp quantification, worms were prepared as described. Image analysis was done with Fiji, where regions of interests were drawn around each worm based on DIC images and mean intensity values of GFP were recorded and plotted.

For daf-7p::gfp quantification, worms were prepared as described. Images were acquired and maximum intensity projections of head neurons were built using Fiji for representative images. Quantification of mean fluorescent intensity was done using NIS Elements software. A single z-stack was selected for analysis that contained the neuron body in the plane of the image. Average pixel intensity was then measured in each worm by drawing a Bezier outline of the neuron cell body for each of the two ASI head neurons, which were independently analyzed. For imaging daf-7p::gfp in each generation, exposure times were adjusted to prevent oversaturation. For control and treatment groups imaged on the same day, the same exposure time and camera settings were used.

### C. elegans survival assay

PF15 was grown in liquid culture overnight (37°C) and diluted 1:2 to an OD = 1. Diluted PF15 or OP50 control (750 μl) was spread to cover six 6-cm NGM plates. Plates were incubated for 2 days at 25°C to allow bacterial growth. N2 worms were bleached using the described protocol onto HG plates seeded with OP50. At 84 hours post-bleach, worms were added to PF15 or OP50 plates equilibrated to 20°C by picking to start the assay. Survival assays were performed at 20°C and assay plates were counted every 6 to 9 hours. Every 48 hours, worms were moved onto new OP50 or PF15 plates prepared as described.

### Quantification of maco-1 gene expression by qPCR

RNA was isolated from F2 progeny of Pfs1 or control-trained P0 worms as described above for whole worm mRNA isolation. Total RNA was extracted using chloroform extraction, isopropanol and ethanol precipitation, and cleanup using the RNeasy mini kit. cDNA was made from 1 μg of RNA using the Superscript III First-strand system for RT-PCR. The extracted cDNA was used as input for qPCR reactions using the Power SYBR green qPCR master mix and protocol and run on a Viia7 Real-time PCR system as previously described (10). The qPCR primers are as follows: maco-1 (forward: GTGTCACGACAATTGCC; reverse: CACATAGGTAGTGGCGAG) and act-1 [forward (43): GGCCCAATCCAAGAGAGGTATC; reverse (43): CAACACGAAGCTCATTGTAGAAGG].

### Statistical analysis

Survival assays were assessed using Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) tests. For choice assays, populations of worms were raised together under identical conditions and were randomly distributed into treatment conditions. For all choice assays, each dot represents an individual choice assay plate (about 15–300 worms per plate). For reversal assays, each dot represents a signal worm. For lysine chemotaxis assays, each dot represents one plate. The box extends from the 25th to the 75 percentiles, with whiskers from the minimum to the maximum values. For the comparison of choice indices between more than two genotypes, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test was used. For comparisons of choice indices between genotypes and between conditions (naïve versus learned), two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test was used. Unpaired, two-tailed Student’s t tests were performed for comparisons between two groups. Experiments were repeated on separate days with separate populations to confirm that results were reproducible. Prism 9 software was used for all statistical analyses.
